Due to health recommendations from the Center for Disease Control and State of California
Division of Occupational Safety and Health (Cal/OSHA), and the declared state of emergency
wherein social distancing measures have been imposed or recommended, the CITY OF
AVALON’S CITY COUNCIL and PLANNING COMMISSION MEETINGS SHALL GENERALLY
BE AVAILABLE TO THE PUBLIC REMOTELY. The general public may attend the meeting in
the Council Chambers however must adhere to social distancing requirements. The public is
encouraged to watch and participate from the safety of their homes while practicing social
distancing.

Chambers reach maximum occupancy, the general public may participate in Oral

admitted into the Council Chambers who is ill or exhibiting symptoms of COVID-19. Additionally,
the general public may participate in Oral Communication and address the City Council on an
agenda items by providing comments via Zoom or by sending comments to
askcityofavalon.com.

3.  Findings to Continue to Hold Remote Teleconferencel’Jirtual City Council Meetings
  Pursuant to Assembly Bill 361
  At the November 16, 2021 City Council meeting, the City Council made findings pursuant
  to Assembly Bill 361 to continue to meet remotely. To continue this practice, it is required,
  that the City Council determine that the COVID-1 9 state of emergency proclaimed by the
  Governor still exists and has been considered by the City Council in deciding to continue
  to have teleconference meetings and that state or local officials have imposed or
  recommended measures to promote social distancing in connection with COVID-19, and
  that as a result of the COVID-19 emergency, meeting in person would present imminent
  risks to the health or safety of attendees. Because these findings must be made every
  thirty (30) days, the City Council will have to make these findings at its upcoming
  November 15, 2022 meeting and thirty (30) days thereafter.
  Recommended Action
  Determine that the COVID-1 9 state of emergency proclaimed by the Governor still exists
  and has been considered by the City Council in deciding to continue to have
  teleconference meetings and that state or local officials have imposed or recommended
  measures to promote social distancing in connection with COVID-19, and that as a result
  of the COVID-19 emergency, meeting in person would present imminent risks to the
  health or safety of attendees.

4.  Award Contract to Olaunu for Year 10 Compliance of the Small Municipal Separate Storm
  Sewer System (MS4) Permit
  The City of Avalon has been designated as a permittee under the Small Municipal
  Separate Storm Sewer System (MS4) Permit. As part of compliance under Year 10 of the
  Small MS4 Permit, the City is responsible for completion of certain requirements.
  Recommended Action
  Approve a contract with Olaunu for a not-to-exceed amount of $52,060 to assist the City
  of Avalon with compliance for Year 10 requirements of the Small Municipal Separate
  Storm Sewer System (MS4) Permit and make the finding that City of Avalon has satisfied
  the sole source requirements as specified in the Avalon Municipal Code (AMC).

PUBLIC HEARING

5.  Appeal of the Decision of the Vehicle Hearing Officer: Denial of a Reguest for an
  Oversized Commercial Autoette
  John Jackson, on behalf of Eagle Electric, submitted an application for a commercial
  autoette permit. The application also indicated Eagle Electric/Jackson was seeking an
  oversized vehicle. The application was considered by the Vehicle Hearing Officer on
  August 19, 2022. As there is no designation for an “oversized” commercial autoette within
  the Avalon Municipal Code, the Vehicle Hearing Officer formally denied the request on
  August 24, 2022.
  Recommended Action
  1. Continue the Public Hearing. 2. Receive Public Comment. 3. Close the Public Hearing.
  4. Consider applicant’s appeal and determine to either a.) Uphold the decision of the
  Vehicle Hearing Officer; or b.) Overturn the decision of the Vehicle Hearing Officer.

6.  Appeal of the Decision of the Vehicle Hearing Officer: Denial of a Request for Transfer of
  a Residential Vehicle Permit
  Margaret Moore submitted an application to transfer a residential vehicle permit (also
  known as a  blue sticker”) to her daughter, Melinda Moore Watson.
  The request was considered by the Vehicle Hearing Officer on August 19, 2022. As
  Melinda Moore Watson is not a current resident as required by the transfer terms the
  request was denied.
  Recommended Action
  1. Open the Public Hearing. 2. Receive Public Comment. 3. Close the Public Hearing. 4.
  Consider applicant’s appeal and determine to either a.) Uphold the decision of the Vehicle
  Hearing Officer; or b.) Overturn the decision of the Vehicle Hearing Officer.

GENERAL BUSINESS

7.  Fiscal Year 2021-22 Year-end Unaudited Financial Results
  The following financial report as of June 30, 2022 is presented for the City Council’s
  review. The purpose of this report is to compare actual revenues and expenditures over
  year-end estimates to provide updated reserve estimates, with the focus on General Fund
  and Harbor Fund activities.
  Recommended Action
  Receive and file the Fiscal Year 2021-22 Year-end Unaudited Financial Results Report.

SUBJECT:  Findings to Continue to Hold Remote TeleconferenceNirtual City
  Council Meetings Pursuant to Assembly Bill 361

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): Determine that the COVID-19 state of emergency proclaimed
by the Governor still exists and has been considered by the City Council in deciding to continue
to have teleconference meetings and that state or local officials have imposed or recommended
measures to promote social distancing in connection with COVID-19, and that as a result of the
COVID-19 emergency, meeting in person would present imminent risks to the health or safety
of attendees.

REPORT SUMMARY: Traditionally, the Brown Act allows for teleconference or virtual meetings,
provided that the physical locations of the legislative body’s members joining by teleconference
are posted on the agenda, that those locations are open to the public and that a quorum of the
members is located within its jurisdiction. Newly enacted AB 361 provides an exception to these
procedures in order to allow for fully virtual meetings during proclaimed emergencies, including
the CO VI D-19 pandemic.

Since March of 2020 and the issuance of Governor Newsom’s Executive Order N-29-20, which
suspended portions of the Brown Act relating to teleconferencing, the City Council has had virtual
meetings without having to post the location of the legislative body members attending virtually.
Most public agencies have been holding public meetings using virtual platforms since this time.
In June of 2021, Governor Newsom issued Executive Order N-08-21, which provided that the
exceptions contained in EO N-29-20 would sunset on September 30, 2021.

On September 10, 2021, the Legislature adopted AB 361, which allows public agencies to hold
fully virtual meetings under certain circumstances without the posting of the agenda from each
location a legislative body member is attending. Governor Newsom signed the bill into law on
September 16, 2021. Because it contained an urgency provision, it took immediate effect.

Specific Findings Required underAB 361

Under AB 361, the City Council can hold virtual meetings without providing notice of the City
Council’s teleconference location if the City Council makes the determination that there is a
Governor-proclaimed state of emergency, which the City Council will consider in their
determination, and one of two secondary criteria listed below exists:

  1. State or local officials have imposed or recommended measures to promote social
  distancing in connection with COVID-19; or

  imminent risk to the health or safety of attendees.

COVID-19 continues to present an imminent threat to the health or safety of members of the
public, and the Governor’s declaration of a COVID-19 emergency still exists. Although vaccines
are now widely available, many people in the State and County are still not fully vaccinated and
remain susceptible to infection. The disease can still spread rapidly through person-to-person
contact and those in close proximity. Further, more contagious variants of the disease are now
present in the State and County, the most predominant of which is a new variant of the Omnicron
variant. The County of Los Angeles recently re-instituted some mandates given the rise in cases
and deaths nationally and public health officials have indicated that they may reinstitute certain
mask requirements if cases continue to rise. The City’s economy is dependent upon visitors to
the island, the presence of which, increases the likelihood of transmission of the disease. Also,
having members of the public attend council meetings at locations where council members are
in attendance due to their desire to avoid exposure to COVID-19 poses an imminent risk to the
health or safety of attendees.

Re-Authorization is Required Within 30 Days

The City Council made the findings listed above at its August 16, 2022 City Council meeting.
Consistent with the provisions of Government Code Section 54953(e), the findings must be made
every 30 days ‘after teleconferencing for the first time” under AS 361. Thus, if the City Council
desires to continue to meet remotely without having to post the location of each teleconference
location, the City Council must again find that the COVID-19 emergency still exists and that one
of the two following findings can be made: that state or local officials have imposed or
recommended measures to promote social distancing in connection with COVID-19, or, that a
result of the COVID-19 emergency, meeting in person would present imminent risks to the health
or safety of attendees. Because these findings must be made every thirty (30) days, the City
Council will have to make these findings at its upcoming November 15, 2022 meeting and thirty
(30) days thereafter.

It is recommended that the City Council make these findings.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: The City Council will
have to follow the Brown Act provisions that existed prior to the COVID-19 pandemic.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: That the City Council make the findings under AS 361 at its November
15, 2022 City Council meeting.

RECOMMENDED ACTION(S): 1. Continue the Public Hearing. 2. Receive Public Comment. 3.

REPORT SUMMARY: The item was initially heard during the October 18, 2022 regular City
Council Meeting. Per City Council direction, the item was continued.

On May 19, 2021, John Jackson, on behalf of Eagle Electric, submitted an application for a new
commercial autoette permit. The application also indicated Eagle Electric/Jackson was seeking
an oversized vehicle. The application was considered by the Vehicle Hearing Officer on August
19, 2022.

As there is no designation for an ‘oversized” commercial autoette within the Avalon Municipal
Code (AMC), the Vehicle Hearing Officer formally denied the request on August 24, 2022. See
findings of fact and conclusions of Law attached hereto.

Per AMC Section 1-4.01 (b), “Except as otherwise specifically provided in this Code, any person
excepting to any decision made by any official of the City Pursuant to any of the provisions of
this Code may appeal in writing to the Council by filing with the City Clerk a written notice of such
appeal setting forth the specific grounds thereof.”

AMC Section 4-4.1703 identifies 9 types of vehicle permits:
  - Residential Vehicle  Public Service/Public Health  and
  - Commercial Vehicle  Safety Vehicle
  - Residential Autoette  -Commercial Rental Autoette
  - Commercial Autoette  Vintage Vehicle
  -

  - Temporary Vehicle  -Horse-Drawn Vehicle

The provisions for granting a commercial autoette permit are defined within AMC Section 4-
4.1703 (c) as follows:
 Commercial Autoette Permits. One commercial autoette permit may be granted to any person,
organization, partnership, trust or corporation for use in connection with a commercial enterprise
located within the City limits or within three miles of the City limits, without being subject to a
waiting period, as follows:

  IlL The following findings must be made in an affirmative manner:
  a. The commercial autoette for which a permit is requested is necessary to the
  proper functioning of the commercial enterprise.
  b. The commercial enterprise has no other vehicle, autoette or other source of
  transportation that can reasonably satisfy its transportation requirements, including
  resident vehicles and autoettes.
  c.That the autoette measures no more than 130 inches in length, including the
  front and rear bumpers.
  d.The commercial enterprise is a significant source of income to the applicant and
  not a side business or hobby, or the Hearing Officer determines that shared use of
  the autoette by two or more businesses owned by the permittee is consistent with
  the purposes and goals of this chapter, or the autoette is to be used on a full-time
  basis or an exclusive basis for a business venture or ventures by the permittee.

The Vehicle Hearing Officer made the finding that Eagle Electric/Jackson is eligible for a
commercial autoette permit. However, the proposed autoette exceeds the maximum length of
an autoette. While the AMC allows for oversized vehicles (Section 4-4.1705.1), it does not allow
for oversized autoettes. In case an autoette does not fulfill the needs of a business, the AMC
allows for a commercial business to apply for a commercial vehicle permit. However, the current
wait list for a commercial vehicle is significant.

In 2021, the City Council discussed autoette size during four regular City Council Meetings.
Discussions resulted in redefining the length of an autoette from 120” to 130”. Additionally, per
City Council direction, autoettes currently registered in the City of Avalon that exceeded the
newly established 130” were granted “grandfathered” status on the condition that they would not
be sold or registered to any other owner in Avalon. At the time the ordinance was adopted, 18
autoettes were “grandfathered” the largest autoette being 143”.
  —

The autoette proposed by Eagle Electric, a Polaris Gem, is 55.5” wide by 146” long.

It should be noted the Polaris Gem does not meet the state established definition of an autoette
and does not comply with the autoette or Low-Speed Vehicle/Neighborhood Electric Vehicle as
defined in either California Vehicle Code 385.5 or 49 CRF 571.500 as existed on January 1,
2010.

City Staff supports the findings of the Vehicle Hearing Officer in as much as the decision is
consistent with the AMC.

GOAL ALIGNMENT: Consistency in application of AMC.
 FISCAL IMPACTS: There is no fiscal impact associated with this action.

CONSEQUENCES OF NOT FOLLOWING RECOMMENDED ACTION: Council action may set
a precedence for larger autoettes throughout Avalon further exacerbating congestion and
parking issues.

FOLLOW UP ACTION: Implement City Council direction.

REPORT SUMMARY: During the February 16, 2021 meeting of the City Council the City
Council had a discussion on autoette lengths as defined by the Avalon Municipal Code (AMC).

During the February 16. 2021 meeting, the City Council directed Staff:
  1. Allow autoettes currently on the Island to receive a ‘special’ temporary permits for a
  period of one year while the City determines exactly how many vehicles do not meet the
  current autoette definition or qualify for the “Low-Speed Vehicle/Neighborhood Electric
  Vehicles” length exemption. Continue gathering data and making an informed analysis,
  and return for next steps.
  2. To not allow any new temporary permits be authorized for vehicles exceeding the length
  requirement as outlined in the AMC. “New permits” would be defined as autoettes not
  previously registered to the City of Avalon.
  3. To not allow resale of Limo autoettes from commercial entities to residents.

  after February 16, 2021.

AMC as well as 115 commercial autoettes utilized for rentals.

Within the AMC, Chapter 4, Section 4.1714, establishes the maximum lengths and widths of
vehicles permitted in Avalon, Per the code:

AUTOETTE  —  Shall mean any of the following: (1) a motor vehicle having three or more
wheels in contact with the ground, an unladen weight of no more than 1,800 pounds and an
overall length of no greater than 120 inches including the front and back bumpers, without
regard to classification or designation of such vehicle by the Department of Motor Vehicles...

The AMC has an autoette length allowance for environmentally friendly “Low-Speed
Vehicle/Neighborhood Electric Vehicles” and a width allowance for “Mica-cars.’

On February 2, 2010, the AMC was amended (Chapter 4, Section 4-4.1705 (b)(1)) to permit
oversized “environmentally friendly vehicles:

An autoette permit may be issued to an otherwise qualified person for an electric-powered
autoette that meets the definition of “Low-Speed Vehicle/Neighborhood Electric Vehicle” as
defined in either California Vehicle Code § 385.5 or 49 CFR 571.500 as it existed on Janua,y
1, 2010, provided such vehicle is registered with the California Department of Motor Vehicles,
has a length of 138 inches or less, including front and rear bumpers, and a width of 67 inches
or less, as measured from the widest part of the vehicle, but not including mirrors or door
handles.”

The AMC was further revised on December 20, 2016 to permit micro-cars (Chapter 4. Section
4-4.1705 (b)(2)):

An autoette permit may be issued to an otherwise qualified person for a SmartForTwo, Scion
or “micro-cars” provided such vehicle is registered as a motor vehicle with the California
Department of Motor Vehicles and has a width of 67 inches or less, as measured from the
widest part of the vehicle, but not including mirrors or door handles and a length no greater
than 120.1 inches.

City Staff have determined that vehicles that exceed the permitted length were previously
permitted for a myriad of reason, including, but not limited to
   -  Rental operators sold oversized autoettes that were approved as commercial vehicles
  or had a full size sticker to residents.
  -  City Staff misinterpreted the vehicle code. (Measuring only the body of the autoette
  versus the full length—  “bumper to bumper” or confusing gas autoettes for “Low

  Speed Vehicles/Neighborhood Electric Vehicles’ as described in the AMC.)
  -  Vehicles were approved as they met the AMC, but later modified to include a rear step,
  additional row of seats or extended bumper.

City Staff is requesting direction from the City Cquncil in how to best proceed with vehicles that
do not meet the requirements as outlined in the AMC.

Potential solutions include:
 1. Amend the AMCto redefine the length of an autoette. (greater than 120 inches)
 2. Prohibit sales arid any new permits for autoettes that exceed the maximum length as
  defined in the AMC, Allow autoettes currently on the island that exceed the maximum

  owner. Once the vehide exceeds its useful life with its current owner, it will be required to

  1. If the total length approved by the AMC is not amended, Staff note this direction

City Staff recommend redefining the length of an autoette to 130 inches. This solution will
address 90% of the autoettes that do not currently conform to the AMC.

Watson.

Section 4-4.1707 (a)(3) of the Avalon Municipal Code (AMC) outlines the terms by which a
residential vehicle permit may be transferred: ‘The permit was issued prior to April 18, 1989 and
is transferred to an adult child of the permittee who is not living with the permittee, and who is a

consistent with the AMC.

Pandemic-related restrictions on outdoor dining and social distancing began to lift during the
development of the Fiscal Year 2021-2022 Budget. In reaction to the ever-changing economic
environment, Staff adopted a conservative approach to revenue projections to aVow for possible
further downturns without significantly disrupting City operations. Revenues ended the fiscal
year up $4.59 million or 38.9% from the adopted budget, driven by transient occupancy tax (TOT)
revenues up $3.55 million from budget estimates. Highlights to significant changes to the City’s
major General Fund revenue sources are outlined below.

Property Tax
Property tax revenues came in $69 thousand higher than year-end estimates and $310 thousand
higher than budget estimates. The increase was primarily driven by underestimated ROPS
residual property tax distributions, which exceeded budget estimates by S244 thousand. ROPS
residual property tax distributions are paid from the Successor Agency’s Redevelopment
Property Tax Trust Fund (RPTTF) and reflect the remaining monies to be distributed after the
Successor Agency’s debt obligations and administrative fees are paid.

Sales Tax
Sales tax revenues include the City’s one percent (1%) share of the current ten percent (10%)
sales tax, the one half percent (05%) add-on sales tax passed through to the Catalina Island
Medical Center, and the City’s share of the one halt percent (0.5%) Public Safety Augmentation
Fund distributed from the County. Sales tax revenues are largely visitor-driven with Restaurants
and Hotels accounting for over half of sales tax revenues. Taxable sales for Restaurants and
Hotels were up 61% compared to Fiscal Year 2020-2021, which operated under significant
 restrictions on bars and indoor dining for most of the fiscal year. Year-end estimates were based
on estimates provided by the City’s sales tax consultant.

Transient Occupancy Tax
Transient Occupancy Tax (TOT) is the largest source of revenues in the General Fund and
accounted for 532% of all General Fund revenues for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2022. TOT
revenues were up $2.68 million or 446% from the prior fiscal year ended June 30, 2021. While
hotel occupancy rates were up from the prior fiscal year, which was impacted with restrictions
on non-essential travel during the winter season, the increase in TOT revenues was primarily
attributable to increases in average room rates resulting in increased tax collections.

Intergovernmental
Intergovernmental revenues primarily consists of $880 thousand from the City’s allocation of
Coronavirus State and Local Fiscal Recovery Funds (SLFR) from the American Rescue Plan
Act, with the remainder from various grant revenues for planning studies and capital projects.
The decrease from budget estimates is attributable to delayed project expenditures to be
reimbursed through grant funding in future years.

Harbor Working Capital

Enterprise funds distinguish between current and noncurrent assets and liabilities. For example,
cash and receivables would be considered current assets and capital assets, such as buildings
and floats, would be considered noncurrent assets. Similarly, payables and accrued liabilities
would be considered current liabilities and pension liabilities and loans payable would be
considered noncurrent liabilities. Because of this distinction, the City is able to calculate working
capital for the Harbor Fund, which is the measure of the City’s ability to meet short-term
obligations.

The City of Avalon adopted new budget and fiscal policies with the Fiscal Year 2021-2022
Budget, including working capital targets for the Harbor Fund. The City’s reserve policy targets
working capital to equal to at least four months of operating expenditures plus an additional
$500,000 for capital outlays or approximately $2.64 million in working capital. The target should
be periodically reconsidered based on certain factors including customer concentration, asset
age and condition, and control over expenses.
